definition: Elegiac means mournfully reflective, expressing sorrow for what is past.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word elegiac. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know elegiac should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The liner's last captain gave an elegiac toast at the scrapyard gate, praising a ship that had outlived the age that built her.
Reflective is milder than elegiac — thoughtful about the past without any note of mourning in it.
Funereal goes further than elegiac — elegiac mourns the past tenderly, while funereal sounds like the funeral itself, heavy and dark.

Mournful means full of plain grief — a mournful face, a mournful tune. Elegiac starts from that grief and adds a tender, backward-looking reflection on something already gone. A funeral procession is mournful; a memoir lingering over a childhood farm long since sold is elegiac.

Valedictory means spoken in farewell — the tone of a goodbye address — and a farewell can be proud or even cheerful. Elegiac is farewell weighted with mourning: sorrow for what is already past. Every elegiac work says goodbye, but many valedictory speeches shed no tears at all.

Elegiac is more than 'sad.' It names a particular tone: grief that looks backward, tender and reflective, for something already gone.
Anger, panic, or fresh raw loss are sad; only the mourning backward look is elegiac.
Elegiac belongs to reviews and essays: it describes art or speech that mourns what is past — tenderly, reflectively, without bitterness.
Plain 'sad' won't do, because elegiac requires the backward look.
Use its unit-mate dirge for the funeral music itself; elegiac is for the tone that mourning leaves on words and images.

The mood is elegiac from the first frame.
Nothing in the pictures is sad in itself — kids on stoops, a grocer weighing plums — but every caption is written in the past tense.
The photographs keep saying, gently, that all of this is gone: the stoops, the grocer, the summer light on brick that no longer stands.

It mourns, she said, but it mourns tenderly, the way you remember a house you can never enter again.
